title: What Is Moralistic Therapeutic Deism? America's Folk Faith
subtitle: The unofficial creed of the American church, left and right, and the five quiet beliefs that replaced the gospel while everyone kept saying the word God.
question: Have we traded the God who died and rose for a distant, agreeable deity who wants us to be nice, exists to make us feel good about ourselves, and stays out of the way until we need him?
whyItMatters: Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton did not set out to name a heresy. Directing the National Study of Youth and Religion, they listened to thousands of American teenagers describe what they actually believed about God, and found that most of them, churched and unchurched, Catholic and Protestant, red state and blue, held the same unspoken creed. In Soul Searching in 2005 they called it moralistic therapeutic deism. It was not printed in any statement of faith. It was what the church had taught by accident, in its songs and its silences, and the young had learned it perfectly. Smith's most unsettling finding was that the teenagers were not rebels. They were echoes. They believed what their parents and their congregations actually believed underneath the official words, and they repeated it back with devastating accuracy. I have preached the official confession from the front and taught the folk religion in everything around it.
biblicalFoundation:
In Soul Searching, Smith and Denton distilled the real creed of American religion into five beliefs. A God exists who created and orders the world and watches over human life. God wants people to be good, nice, and fair to each other, as most religions teach. The central goal of life is to be happy and to feel good about oneself. God does not need to be particularly involved in one's life except when he is needed to resolve a problem. And good people go to heaven when they die. Read them again slowly. Every one of them is almost true, and not one of them is the gospel.

Begin with the deism, the first belief and the fourth, which together describe a God who set the world spinning and then withdrew, available on request. Smith memorably described this God as something like a combination divine butler and cosmic therapist, there to meet needs and smooth feelings and otherwise keep his distance. But the God of Scripture did not order the world and step back from it. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us. He is Immanuel, God with us, who entered his own creation and bled inside it. My thoughts are not your thoughts, he says through Isaiah, neither are your ways my ways. The domesticated deity of the folk faith is not a smaller version of that God. He is a different one.

Then the moralism, the second belief, that God chiefly wants us to be good, nice, and fair. Niceness is not holiness, and the two are often enemies. Jesus was not nice. He overturned tables and called respectable men whitewashed tombs, and he set a standard that manners cannot touch. You therefore must be perfect, he said, as your heavenly Father is perfect. The law was never a code of pleasantness. It exposes us and drives us to mercy, which is the last thing niceness thinks it needs.

Then the therapeutic, the third belief, that the central goal of life is to be happy and to feel good about oneself. Against that stands the hardest arithmetic Jesus ever taught. Whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will save it. The gospel does not aim at my self-esteem. It aims at my death and my resurrection, and it will not settle for improving the self it means to crucify.

And the fifth belief is the oldest lie of all, that good people go to heaven when they die. It sounds like the whole point of religion, and it is the exact thing the cross exists to deny. None is righteous, no, not one. For by grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not your own doing, it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast. If good people went to heaven for being good, then Christ died for nothing. The fifth tenet does not add a little works-righteousness to the gospel. It empties the cross and keeps the word salvation as a souvenir.

churchRecord.led: At its best the church has refused every domestication of God. It confessed a Lord, not a butler, and a grace that costs everything, not a reward for being pleasant. The creeds were written precisely to keep the faith from dissolving into the surrounding culture's assumptions, and the martyrs proved that the thing they believed was worth more than their comfort or their lives. Whenever the church has been most alive, it has insisted that God makes total claims and not helpful suggestions.
churchRecord.failed: But moralistic therapeutic deism did not sneak past the church. The church manufactured it. We built youth ministries on entertainment and called it discipleship, preached sermons that were life tips with a verse stapled on, sang songs that never once mentioned sin, and trimmed God down to something useful and safe. Smith's teenagers did not invent this creed. They learned it from us, precisely, and handed it back. I have taught the official confession from the pulpit and the folk religion in everything surrounding it.

whereWeAgree: God did create and order the world, and he does want a real goodness, and he does meet us in our trouble, and there is a heaven. Every tenet of this folk faith is a truth with its spine removed. That is exactly what makes it so hard to confront. You cannot refute it by denying its sentences, because the sentences are nearly right. You have to show what each one quietly leaves out, and what it costs a person to leave it out.
captureLeft: On the left the deism becomes a God who is pure affirmation, the cosmic endorsement of my conscience and my causes, a love that blesses whatever I already am and would never presume to call me to change. He is present to celebrate me and absent to correct me. The offense of the cross is retired as primitive, and what remains is a spirituality that asks nothing and rules nothing out.
captureRight: On the right the same deism becomes a God of country and personal blessing, a divine sponsor of the flag, the family, and the upward arc of the respectable life. He rewards hard work and good citizenship and keeps a comfortable distance otherwise. The offense of the cross recedes behind self-improvement and civil religion, and what remains is a faith that flatters the nation and the self.
whereWeDiffer: We part from both because a God trimmed to be useful has already stopped being God. The Lord of Scripture is not a butler waiting in the wings for emergencies, and not a therapist whose assignment is my self-esteem. He is the God who became flesh, who was crucified for sins that are actually mine, who rose in a body from a real grave, and who calls me to die and be raised with him. That God cannot be reduced to a life enhancement. He can only be worshiped or refused.
theCost: To preach against this is to disappoint almost everyone, because almost everyone, left and right, is quietly counting on the folk faith. It costs a congregation the reassurance that they are fine as they are and that being decent is enough. It means telling good people that being good will not save them, which may be the least welcome sentence in the American church. It is easier, every single Sunday, to bless the deism and send everyone home comfortable and unconverted.
charge: Stop asking whether God is useful to you and start asking whether he is Lord. Find the tenet of the folk faith you have been living inside, the nice God, the distant God, the God who exists to make you feel good about yourself, and hold it up against the God who hung on a cross. Then tell the truth gently to someone who has only ever been handed the butler, and stay beside them while the real God turns out to be larger and more demanding, and far more worth having, than the one they thought they had.

right.label: God, Country, and the Self-Help Almighty
right.whatItLooksLike: On the right, moralistic therapeutic deism dresses in God and country and personal improvement. God blesses the flag, rewards the hard worker, and underwrites the respectable American life. Faith becomes a source of confidence and a sanctifier of the nation, a civil religion that makes the country holy and a self-help program that makes the self succeed. He keeps a polite distance, on call for emergencies, and the cross recedes behind the promise of a better and more upright life.
right.inThePast: The synthesis was built in the mid-twentieth century, when the words under God were added to the Pledge of Allegiance in 1954 and In God We Trust was adopted as the national motto in 1956, binding a generic deity to national identity. Norman Vincent Peale fused popular psychology with Christian language in The Power of Positive Thinking in 1952, and God became, for millions, the sponsor of confidence and success.
right.now: The stream runs on in a suburban evangelicalism where God underwrites the family, the nation, and the personal brand, and where faith is measured by how much better it makes an ordinary life. The deism is fully intact. God created and ordered a world he now mostly leaves to run itself, appearing to bless the enterprise and to solve the occasional crisis, keeping his respectful distance the rest of the week.

left.label: God as the Endorsement of My Values
left.whatItLooksLike: On the left, the same deism dresses in affirmation and conscience. God is the warm endorsement of my values, a love that only ever agrees, who blesses my compassion and my causes and would never presume to judge. Faith becomes self-acceptance with a sacred glow, a spirituality that asks nothing and forbids nothing. He keeps a flattering distance, present to celebrate and absent to correct, and the cross recedes behind the promise of a kinder and more enlightened self.
left.inThePast: The lineage runs through liberal Protestantism, whose God H. Richard Niebuhr described in 1937 as one without wrath, bringing men without sin into a kingdom without judgment through a Christ without a cross. Robert Bellah found the same faith privatized in 1985, in the woman he called Sheila, who named her gentle, self-derived religion after herself, a God shrunk to fit one conscience.
left.now: The stream runs on in a progressive spirituality where God is the cosmic affirmation of my politics and my self-acceptance, and in the exvangelical drift that leaves a rigid system for a faith that asks nothing in return. Tara Isabella Burton mapped the remixed, self-authored religions of the moment in Strange Rites. The deism is fully intact. God exists to validate the self and otherwise keeps a respectful distance.
